processing: Raw pu-erh pressed into cakes at a state factory. Green-cake and iron-pressed versions are both listed in auctions.
harvest_season: Not recorded. Spring leaf is generally the most prized in pu-erh.
appearance_dry: Aged brown cakes with a wrapper identified by yellow as its mark colour.
appearance_liquor: Deep amber, as is usual for raw pu-erh aged for several decades.
appearance_wet: Brown, softened leaf, typical of raw pu-erh of this age.
taste_profile: Few dependable tasting notes exist. Raw pu-erh of this age typically tastes of wood and earth with some remaining sweetness.

brewing.notes: General advice for aged raw pu-erh, with a brief rinse and short early steeps.

vintage_note: Sold by rough decade, and the dating is loose. Auction listings include 1960s Eight Zhong Yellow Mark green cakes and 1970s iron cakes, and the 1970s Qizi Yellow Mark is also named. Ask exactly which version is meant.
description:
Yellow Mark is among the named mark teas, the state-factory raw pu-erh cakes known by a colour on their packaging. It is less celebrated than Red Mark or Blue Mark and it comes later in the story.

It also sits close to the end of the mark era. The name covers more than one product, so it is more useful as a collector's label than as a recipe.

Little has been recorded about its cup. Expect what raw pu-erh of this age generally offers, wood and earth with some sweetness, and brew it with hot water and short steeps.

When buying, pin down the decade and version. Many modern cakes borrowing mark names have no link to the originals, and the wrapper name is not proof of age.
history:
Yellow Mark is usually placed in the later mark period, not the 1950s. Auction catalogues list both 1960s and 1970s versions, and it has been linked to the Menghai 7542 line of the 1970s.

Which factory made each version and how much it made are poorly documented. Dates quoted for it should be taken as market conventions unless a catalogue can back them up.
